storm.summary_layperson: A Thanksgiving nor'easter is bringing steady heavy rain, strong northeast winds gusting past 30 knots, and coastal flooding at high tide tonight — no thunderstorms, and the Sound offers no protection in this setup.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the Sound (53°F) is about 14°F warmer than the air, and the gap only narrows to ~10°F by 8 PM — it never flips into the protective cool-water setup.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a coastal storm (nor'easter) is moving up the coast. Radar shows a broad shield of moderate rain (35–40 dBZ) covering the whole area within 15 miles of the cove, drifting slowly east at about 5 kt. This is widespread steady rain, not thunderstorms — there is zero instability (CAPE 0 J/kg) despite very strong winds aloft (73 kt of shear), so lightning and hail are not expected. RYC is already logging rain at 0.27 in/hr, and NWS expects ¾ to 1 inch of new rain.

Active NWS alerts: a Coastal Flood Warning runs until 6 AM Friday and a Wind Advisory until 1 AM, with a Coastal Flood Advisory following Friday morning. Hours of onshore northeast wind are piling water into western Long Island Sound — the flooding risk around tonight's high tide is the most important hazard for the waterfront, more than the rain itself.

Local modifier — none in play: the cove's usual protection comes from cool Sound water under warm air, which forms a stable layer that weakens incoming storms. Tonight it's the reverse: the water (53°F) is warmer than the air (~39–43°F). The forecast air temperature rises slowly through the evening, closing the gap from about 14°F to 10°F by 8 PM, but the water stays warmer the entire time, so there is no stable layer and no buffer. The sea breeze is also out of the picture — sunset was 4:28 PM and this is a strong storm-driven wind.

Arrival of the next heavier band: the closest heavier rain cell is about 3 miles WNW, creeping toward the cove; expect it around 5:15 PM (window 4:50–5:35 PM, medium confidence). With no local effects to slow or weaken it, the arrival timing is purely the storm's own motion. Expect a burst of heavier rain and gusts, not a thunderstorm.

Cove vs. surrounding areas: conditions here will be essentially the same as Stamford, Rye, and the Long Island north shore — wind-driven rain, gusts around 30 kt (NWS has gusts up to 55 mph possible in exposed spots), and minor-to-moderate coastal flooding in low-lying waterfront areas.

What would change the call: a warning for severe thunderstorms or flash flooding, or radar echoes intensifying above 45 dBZ near the cove, would push this to high risk. The model and the NWS forecast both keep the wind going strong past midnight, so don't expect the storm to ease off within the evening.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked heavier rain band 3 mi WNW drifting east at ~5 kt; no marine-layer buffer tonight, so expect a burst of heavy rain and gusts at full strength — no thunder.

wind.regime_label: Strong northeast storm wind — no sea breeze
wind.tactics_blurb: No racing tonight — this is a nor'easter after dark with a Wind Advisory and gusts near 30+ kt. If anything is on the water, the northeast breeze is fairly even across the cove, slightly stronger mid-cove: stay center.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The call: this is a strong gradient-wind day — a coastal storm, not a sea breeze. The air is about 14°F colder than the Sound (53°F water vs. ~39°F inland air), so there is no thermal driver at all, and sunset was at 4:28 PM, before the window opens. The authoritative stations average about 17 kt with gusts into the 30s, and NWS has a Wind Advisory until 1 AM. Storm wind doesn't care about the sun: it holds through the whole evening.

Cove numbers: the model (HRRR) puts open-water wind at 22–27 kt from the NE this evening, but RYC is reading 14 kt sustained (13 kt over 10 minutes) with gusts to 28 kt — the cove sits in the lee of the land in a northeast wind, so it runs about a third lighter than the model's open-water number. The table scales the model accordingly: 15–18 kt sustained, gusts 28–33 kt, with gusts nearly double the average — very puffy.

Direction and shifts: northeast throughout, veering slowly from about 45° to 55° through the evening. RYC agrees (NE 38°), but stations just east of the cove along Old Greenwich are reading more easterly (one at E 24 kt gusting 35), so expect the breeze to swing between NE and ENE in the bigger gusts. The model's hourly run stops at 8 PM; the 9 and 10 PM rows assume the storm wind simply carries on, which the NWS forecast supports.

Where the pressure is: in northeast flow the breeze is fairly even across the cove, slightly stronger mid-cove than tight against either shore. Center is favored.

What it feels like: 15–18 kt average with 30+ kt gusts, heavy rain, darkness, and air around 42°F is beyond racing conditions for any small-boat fleet and is a survival-and-check-your-mooring night for keelboats. Coastal flooding at high tide is a bigger concern for boats and docks than the wind itself.

data_caveats: Model hourly wind only reaches 8 PM (later forecast hours unavailable); 9 PM and 10 PM rows are extrapolated by persistence, backed by the NWS forecast and Wind Advisory through 1 AM
Western Long Island Sound buoy 44040 offline (UConn data server returned 404) — no over-water wind or temperature
Several airport stations (Bridgeport, New Haven, Islip, Farmingdale, Westhampton) reporting gusts but no sustained wind — sensors excluded from the wind averages
Cove wind speeds scaled down from the model's open-water values to match RYC, which reads about a third lighter in northeast flow
